results.authors: Postuma RB, Berg D, Stern M, et al.
results.summary: The MDS criteria require parkinsonism (bradykinesia plus rest tremor or rigidity) as an entry criterion, followed by supportive criteria, absolute exclusion criteria, and red flags. In young-onset cases (age <50), Wilson's disease must be excluded. Clinically established PD requires at least 2 supportive criteria and no exclusion criteria or red flags. Clear levodopa response is a major supportive criterion.
results.title: MDS Clinical Diagnostic Criteria for Parkinson's Disease

results.authors: Tolosa E, Garrido A, Scholz SW, Poewe W
results.summary: Young-onset Parkinson's disease (onset before age 50) accounts for 5-10% of all PD cases and is more frequently associated with monogenic causes, particularly PRKN (Parkin) mutations (most common genetic cause of young-onset PD), PINK1, DJ-1, and LRRK2. Genetic counseling and panel testing should be offered. The differential of young-onset parkinsonism includes Wilson's disease (serum ceruloplasmin, 24-h urine copper, slit-lamp for KF rings), dopa-responsive dystonia (therapeutic levodopa trial), and functional movement disorder. DaTscan confirms presynaptic dopaminergic deficit in uncertain cases.
results.title: Challenges in the Diagnosis of Parkinson's Disease

results.summary: Updated discussion of MDS criteria application in young-onset and genetic PD. Emphasizes that idiopathic and monogenic PD share identical clinical criteria application. DaTscan is particularly valuable in young patients where clinical features overlap with essential tremor and dystonic tremor.
results.title: The New Diagnostic Criteria for Parkinson's Disease

prohibited_recommendations: Do not dismiss the clinical syndrome as functional or anxiety-related solely because the patient is young (42 years) — young-onset PD is a well-established entity and this patient has objective signs of parkinsonism with an abnormal DaTscan
Do not skip Wilson's disease exclusion in a patient under 50 with parkinsonism — Wilson's disease is treatable with chelation and failure to identify it is a serious clinical error
Do not prescribe dopamine receptor antagonists (typical or atypical antipsychotics, metoclopramide, prochlorperazine, promethazine) — these will worsen parkinsonism and confound diagnosis
Do not prescribe typical antipsychotics or most atypical antipsychotics for any behavioral indication; if antipsychotic therapy is required, restrict to quetiapine, clozapine, or pimavanserin
Do not use anticholinergic agents (trihexyphenidyl, benztropine) as primary therapy given the long anticipated disease course and cognitive side-effect risk in a young patient
required_recommendations: Exclude Wilson's disease in this patient with young-onset parkinsonism (age <50): obtain serum ceruloplasmin, serum copper, 24-hour urinary copper, and slit-lamp examination for Kayser-Fleischer rings — Wilson's disease is treatable and must not be missed

Apply MDS 2015 clinical diagnostic criteria for Parkinson's disease: parkinsonism (bradykinesia plus rest tremor and rigidity), supportive criteria (micrographia, asymmetric onset, rest tremor, probable abnormal DaTscan), no absolute exclusion criteria, no red flags
Offer genetic counseling and PD-gene panel testing (PRKN/PARK2, PINK1, DJ-1, LRRK2, GBA, SNCA) given young-onset — monogenic PD is common in this age group and has implications for family members

Do not dismiss as functional movement disorder on the basis of age alone — true rest tremor, cogwheel rigidity, bradykinesia, and micrographia with abnormal DaTscan establish an organic presynaptic dopaminergic deficit
Confirm levodopa responsiveness as a supportive criterion for PD diagnosis (clear and dramatic benefit to adequate dose is the strongest supportive criterion per MDS 2015)
Review full medication list to exclude dopamine receptor antagonists as a cause of parkinsonism before finalizing diagnosis

key_clinical_evidence: Young-onset parkinsonism (age <50) mandates Wilson's disease exclusion before any other diagnosis is accepted — Wilson's disease is rare but treatable, and its parkinsonism is clinically indistinguishable from idiopathic PD

Normal serum ceruloplasmin (28 mg/dL), normal serum copper (88 microg/dL), normal 24-h urinary copper (28 microg/24h), and absence of Kayser-Fleischer rings collectively and definitively exclude Wilson's disease in this case

DaTscan showing reduced LEFT putaminal uptake (contralateral to the clinically worse RIGHT side) confirms a presynaptic dopaminergic deficit and is inconsistent with functional movement disorder or dopa-responsive dystonia
The 'too young for PD' cognitive anchor is the primary red herring — young-onset PD (onset <50) accounts for 5-10% of all PD cases and follows identical MDS 2015 diagnostic criteria

Genetic testing (PRKN/Parkin biallelic mutations are the most common monogenic cause of young-onset PD) should be offered regardless of family history, as de novo mutations occur and recessive inheritance may not manifest in family members
In young patients, dopamine agonists are typically preferred as initial therapy over levodopa to delay motor complications given the longer anticipated treatment duration

patient.history_present_illness: Mr. Carlos Vega is a 42-year-old right-handed software engineer who presents to the movement disorders clinic accompanied by his wife for evaluation of a progressive right hand tremor and generalized slowness of movement over the past 14 months. He first noticed a subtle intermittent shakiness of his right hand approximately 14 months ago while sitting at his desk and resting his hand on the keyboard. He initially attributed it to overuse and stress. Over subsequent months, the tremor became more persistent, occurring predominantly at rest while watching television or during meetings, and temporarily disappearing when he reached purposefully for an object. His wife noticed the tremor during a family dinner approximately eight months ago, when his hand was resting on the table, and she encouraged him to seek medical attention. He reports progressive right arm stiffness that has affected his work performance — he now makes significantly more typing errors and has slowed considerably at the keyboard. He describes difficulty with right-hand fine motor tasks including handling coins, fastening buttons, and using a screwdriver. He has noticed his right arm does not swing naturally when walking. He reports that his handwriting has become noticeably smaller over the past six months, to the point where his wife and colleagues have commented on it. Over the past four months, he has experienced a pervasive feeling of right-sided fatigue and heaviness that he describes as distinct from muscular tiredness. He has had no frank falls, though he reports feeling mildly unsteady when turning quickly. He notes mild constipation emerging over the past six months requiring increased fiber intake, and occasional episodes of waking from vivid dreams. His wife reports he has acted out a dream on two occasions over the past three months, waving his arm during sleep. He denies visual hallucinations, cognitive changes, dysphagia, or significant orthostatic symptoms. He was seen by his primary care physician three months ago who attributed the tremor to 'anxiety and occupational overuse' and recommended stress management; he was not started on any neurological medications. He denies any exposure to antipsychotics, antiemetics, or other dopamine-blocking agents. He has no prior history of liver disease, psychiatric illness, or toxic exposures. There is no family history of Parkinson's disease or Wilson's disease.

neurological_exam.additional: Handwriting sample shows micrographia with progressive letter compression. Glabellar tap reflex positive (non-habituating). No myoclonus. No alien limb phenomenon. No cortical sensory deficits. No apraxia. Slit-lamp examination: cornea clear bilaterally, no Kayser-Fleischer rings identified.
neurological_exam.coordination: Finger-to-nose testing intact bilaterally without dysmetria. Heel-to-shin testing normal. No intentional tremor. Rapid alternating movements markedly impaired on the right with decrement (bradykinesia); left mildly impaired.
neurological_exam.cranial_nerves: Pupils equal, round, and reactive to light bilaterally. Extraocular movements full without nystagmus. No Kayser-Fleischer rings noted on slit-lamp biomicroscopy performed at presentation. Facial expression mildly reduced with decreased blink rate. Hearing grossly intact. Palate elevates symmetrically. Sternocleidomastoid and trapezius strength 5/5. Tongue midline without fasciculations or atrophy.
neurological_exam.gait: Mildly stooped posture. Reduced right arm swing. Stride length mildly shortened. En bloc turning requiring 4-5 steps for 180-degree turn. Mild hesitancy on gait initiation. Pull test: 1-2 steps retropulsion, self-corrects. No festination. Tandem gait mildly impaired.
neurological_exam.mental_status: Alert and fully oriented. Speech is mildly hypophonic but fluent, grammatically correct, and with intact comprehension, naming, and repetition. MoCA 29/30 (lost 1 point on delayed recall). No evidence of cognitive impairment. Clock drawing normal.
neurological_exam.motor: Bulk normal throughout. Tone: cogwheel rigidity at the right wrist and right elbow, accentuated with activation maneuver. Mild lead-pipe rigidity at the right ankle. Left-sided tone normal. Strength 5/5 in all extremities. No pronator drift. Bradykinesia is prominent in the right hand — finger tapping shows marked slowing with progressive amplitude decrement. Left hand tapping mildly slow but preserved amplitude. Right foot tapping mildly slow. Resting tremor of the right hand at 4-5 Hz, pill-rolling in character, present at rest and with distraction tasks, suppressed with purposeful movement and re-emerging after a latency. No tremor observed in left hand, chin, or lower extremities.
neurological_exam.reflexes: 2+ and symmetric at bilateral biceps, triceps, brachioradialis, and patellar tendons. Achilles 2+ bilaterally. Plantar responses flexor bilaterally. No Hoffmann sign. No clonus.
neurological_exam.sensory: Intact to light touch, pinprick, temperature, vibration, and proprioception throughout all four extremities. No sensory level.
